c.tagline: A remote Western Desert oasis of mudbrick ruins, salt lakes, and the ancient Oracle of Amun that Alexander the Great once consulted

taxi.fareNote: Most sightseeing is arranged as a half or full-day tour with a local driver

emergency.note: Tourist police can assist; English support is limited this far from major resorts

walk: The town center and Shali Fortress are walkable; the salt lakes, springs, and Great Sand Sea require a car or guided excursion

safety.safety: Generally calm and welcoming; check current travel advisories for this part of Egypt's Western Desert before visiting
safety.crime: Low crime; the main risks relate to desert travel and remoteness rather than crime

hood_landmark.Shali Town Center: The Shali Fortress ruins towering over the modern town
hood_landmark.Temple of the Oracle (Aghurmi): The Temple of the Oracle of Amun
hood_landmark.Great Sand Sea (day-trip base): The rolling dunes of the Great Sand Sea

avoid.reason: Western desert near the Libya border — outlying areas restricted; travel with permits/guides

hood_desc: The heart of modern Siwa beneath the crumbling mudbrick Shali Fortress, with most guesthouses, restaurants, and the market.
A short ride from town, home to the ancient oracle temple where Alexander the Great reportedly sought confirmation of his divinity.
The vast dune sea south of town, reached by 4x4 for sandboarding, dune-bashing, and overnight desert camps.

water.note: Drink bottled water; the oasis's brackish groundwater is not potable.

transit.sys: Local taxis and guide-arranged 4x4 vehicles; no formal bus network within Siwa
transit.pay: Cash to the driver or guide
transit.map: Not centrally published; guesthouses arrange transport
transit.note: Bicycles are a popular and pleasant way to get around central Siwa itself

transport.air: No airport in Siwa; Marsa Matruh Airport is the nearest, about 3 hr away by road
transport.bus: Long-distance buses connect Siwa to Alexandria and Cairo (8-11 hr journey)
transport.car: The Marsa Matruh-Siwa road is the main route in; a guide is recommended for any off-road desert travel

net.m: Limited 3G/4G in town, no coverage in the desert
net.w: Wifi available in some guesthouses but often slow
net.ops: Vodafone Egypt, Orange Egypt, Etisalat Misr
net.fwn: Wifi available in central guesthouses, though unreliable
net.ap: A Vodafone or Orange Egypt tourist SIM or eSIM

tip.s: 10% is customary and appreciated for desert guides
tip.r: Rounding up or 5-10% is appreciated, not obligatory

food.name: Tagilla, Siwan sand bread
food.desc: A dense wheat loaf baked in hot sand and ash, then torn up and eaten with olive oil and crushed dates; the oldest thing on any Siwan table.

places.name: Abdu Restaurant
places.note: The town's best-known kitchen since the 1980s; Siwan versions of Egyptian staples.

places.name: Albabenshal
places.note: Built into the old mudbrick town; rooftop tables and traditional Siwan cooking.

places.name: Taziry Ecolodge
places.note: Kettle-and-sand baking done on site as part of the lodge's Siwan kitchen.

food.name: Siwan dates
food.desc: Saidy and frafra dates from the oasis groves, recognised by Slow Food; eaten fresh, sun-dried, pressed into paste or stuffed with almonds.

places.name: Siwa central market
places.note: Stalls sell every local variety loose by the kilo, plus date paste and syrup.

places.name: Siwa Community Development date workshops
places.note: Local cooperatives selling packed dates, date sugar and preserves made in the oasis.

places.name: Abdu Restaurant
places.note: Famous for its date pancakes filled and topped with heavy date jam.

food.name: Siwan olives and olive oil
food.desc: The oasis presses some of Egypt's best oil; olives arrive cured and salty as a first course, the oil poured over everything from bread to eggs.

places.name: Siwa central market
places.note: Barrels of cured olives and bottles of new-press oil sold straight from the growers.

places.name: Local olive presses on the Maraqi road
places.note: Working presses open to visitors during the autumn harvest.

places.name: Albabenshal
places.note: Serves olives and oil as the standard opener with Siwan bread.

food.name: Agroz, palm heart salad
food.desc: The tender core of a felled date palm, sliced thin and dressed with lemon and olive oil - crisp, faintly sweet, and only available when a tree comes down.

places.name: Abdu Restaurant
places.note: One of the few restaurants that puts agroz on the menu when it is available.

places.name: Kenooz Shali
places.note: Traditional Siwan house restaurant with seasonal oasis dishes.

places.name: Taziry Ecolodge
places.note: Cooks from its own palm groves and gardens; agroz appears in season.

food.name: Lamb fattah and slow-cooked stews
food.desc: Layers of rice and toasted bread under lamb and garlicky broth, or lamb simmered for hours with tomato and cumin - the feast food of Siwan weddings.

places.name: Abdu Restaurant
places.note: Reliable for the heavier cooked dishes as well as the vegetarian Siwan staples.

places.name: Tekeyet Elamir Restaurant and Cafe
places.note: Popular local sit-down spot for grills, stews and Egyptian classics.

places.name: Adrere Amellal
places.note: Candlelit desert lodge serving set Siwan menus built around slow-cooked lamb.

food.name: Tarfant and elhuji
food.desc: Two Siwan breakfasts: bread soaked in olive oil with dates, and eggs fried in olive oil then mashed together with date paste. Sweet, salty and very old.

places.name: Abdu Restaurant
places.note: Date-and-oil breakfasts plus the date pancakes it is known for.

places.name: Albabenshal
places.note: Breakfast on the roof over the ruins, with local bread, oil and dates.

places.name: Shali Lodge
places.note: Garden lodge kitchen serving Siwan breakfast to guests and walk-ins.

food.name: Karkade hibiscus tea
food.desc: Deep red hibiscus steeped and sweetened, poured hot in winter and iced in summer; served with the sage or mint infusions that follow every Siwan meal.

places.name: Tekeyet Elamir Restaurant and Cafe
places.note: Cafe as much as restaurant; hibiscus and herbal teas served all day.

places.name: Siwa central market cafes
places.note: Traditional tea houses around the square where men sit over karkade and shai.

places.name: Albabenshal
places.note: Rooftop tea at sunset over the mudbrick ruins.

food.name: Siwa date juice
food.desc: Dates blended with milk or water into a thick, sweet shake, sometimes with banana or almond; the oasis answer to a soft drink, and served everywhere.

places.name: Abdu Restaurant
places.note: Date shakes and juices alongside the famous date pancakes.

places.name: Juice stalls on the main square
places.note: Fresh date, mango and sugarcane juices pressed to order.

places.name: Kenooz Shali
places.note: Serves date drinks and herbal infusions in a traditional Siwan setting.

landmarks: Shali Fortress
The dreamlike ruined citadel of old Siwa, a melted-looking labyrinth of kershef salt-mud towers rising above the town, magical at sunset.
Temple of the Oracle of Amun
The hilltop temple at Aghurmi where Alexander the Great consulted the famed oracle in 331 BC and was hailed as son of Amun.
Cleopatra's Spring (Ain Juba)
A round stone-walled natural spring bubbling with clear water amid palm groves, Siwa's most famous swimming spot since antiquity.
Mountain of the Dead (Gebel al-Mawta)
A honeycombed conical hill of rock-cut tombs from Egypt's 26th Dynasty and Ptolemaic era, several still vivid with painted scenes.
Fatnas Island
A palm-shaded islet on the salt lake of Birket Siwa, celebrated for hibiscus tea and Siwa's most spectacular lake sunsets.
Great Sand Sea
An ocean of towering dunes stretching to Libya, explored from Siwa by 4x4 for dune-bashing, sandboarding, fossil beds and desert hot springs.
Siwa Salt Lakes
Startlingly turquoise salt pools with white crystal shores where bathers float effortlessly, the oasis's most surreal photo backdrop.
Bir Wahed
A hot spring and adjacent cold freshwater pool on the edge of the Great Sand Sea, perfect for a starlit desert soak.
Temple of Umm Ubayda
The toppled remains of a 30th-Dynasty temple to Amun, once linked to the Oracle temple by sacred processional way, with hieroglyph-covered blocks.
Dakrour Mountain
A twin-peaked hill famed for therapeutic hot-sand baths and as the gathering place of Siwa's annual Siyaha reconciliation festival.

train.note: There is no railway to Siwa - it sits deep in the Western Desert near the Libyan border, about 300 km from the coast. Egyptian National Railways' nearest line reaches Marsa Matruh on the Mediterranean, roughly four hours north by road. Everyone arrives by bus or private car.

bus.note: No international coaches - the Libyan border here is closed to travellers. West & Middle Delta Bus Company runs from Siwa to Marsa Matruh in about 4 hours, continuing to Alexandria in 8-9 and Cairo in 10-12, with only a couple of departures a day. Buy at the Siwa bus office a day ahead, as seats are limited. Shared microbuses cover the Matruh run more frequently.

ferry.note: Siwa is a desert oasis some 300 km from the sea and 18 m below sea level, so there are no ferries. The salt lakes around the oasis are for floating in, not for boats.

full.name: Qara Oasis
full.blurb: Tiny, isolated oasis village on the edge of the Qattara Depression, reached by desert track.

full.name: Marsa Matruh
full.blurb: Mediterranean coastal city with white-sand beaches, reached via the paved desert highway north of Siwa.
